Marathon Petroleum's stock has dropped sharply over the past week—down nearly 1.5% over two weeks and falling steeply since November 13—despite refineries running at a healthy 95.7% capacity. The core problem is oil prices: US crude has fallen to $89.53 per barrel, and that lower feedstock cost directly shrinks refiner profit margins (the difference between what they pay for crude and what they earn selling refined products). At the same time, storage levels for gasoline and diesel remain elevated, which signals weak demand and puts additional pressure on the prices refiners can charge.

The geopolitical uncertainty around Iran and the Strait of Hormuz, while historically bullish for oil prices, hasn't been enough to offset the demand weakness reflected in those stockpiles. The broader market concern—visible in energy sector weakness—appears to be that slowing or stalled economic growth will keep fuel consumption depressed, squeezing refiner economics even as they run at full tilt.
